zone: Azurite Peak and Mount Ballard — Mill Creek and the West Fork Methow
_areas_note: ONE PEAK REMOVED. Wolframite Mountain is not part of this group and shares nothing with it. It stands in the far north-eastern Pasayten close to the Canadian border, is climbed off the Boundary Trail near Apex Pass, and is reached from the Chewuch and Toats Coulee road system out of Winthrop or Loomis — a drive of several hours from anything in this file and a completely different drainage. Its coordinate confirms it: it sits well over thirty miles north-east of Azurite. It belongs with the eastern Pasayten trailhead cluster, not here. What remains is a genuine pair. Azurite Peak and Mount Ballard stand about two miles apart on the same ridge and are almost always climbed on the same trip, and TWO approaches of roughly equal length serve both, from opposite sides. (1) From the west, the Canyon Creek trailhead on SR 20 near milepost 141, up Canyon Creek to the Mill Creek trail, past the old Azurite Mine, to Azurite Pass. (2) From the east, the Lost River Road and the lower Harts Pass road out of Mazama, up the West Fork Methow and Brush Creek to the same pass. Both are long, both are on trails in poor repair, and neither is a weekend outing for a casual party. This is Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest throughout and it is NOT the national park — no backcountry permit applies to either peak. The designated Pasayten Wilderness boundary lies to the north, and a trail from the Canyon Creek trailhead does head that way, so a trip that wanders north picks up the free self-issue wilderness permit; the Azurite and Ballard approaches themselves do not. Nothing here duplicates the Harts Pass file, which covers the high campgrounds at the pass itself and the trailheads twenty road miles further up; these are the low valley camps below all of that.

sites.name: Canyon Creek trailhead, SR 20
sites.capacity: A large parking area just east of milepost 141, roughly a third of the way between Newhalem and Rainy Pass. Rarely busy, because almost nobody uses the trail these peaks need.
sites.water: No potable water at the trailhead. Canyon Creek is close by and needs filtering.
sites.permit: No camping permit. Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass to park. This is national forest and there is no quota or reservation of any kind. A separate trail from this same lot runs north into the Pasayten Wilderness, which does carry a free self-issue permit from the kiosk, so read the board and take one only if your route actually crosses that boundary.
sites.notes: This is the western door to Azurite and Ballard, and the drive alone puts it a long way from anywhere — roughly thirty-three miles east of Marblemount and sixteen west of Rainy Pass, with no services in either direction. Parties commonly sleep in the lot before starting, and the low elevation means it is warm and buggy in early summer when the peaks above are still white. The trail from here runs about six miles up Canyon Creek before the Mill Creek trail branches right at around two thousand eight hundred feet, a third of a mile past the trail's own crossing of Mill Creek. The whole point of understanding this trailhead is the arithmetic that follows: the pass is around six thousand seven hundred feet and the car is at nineteen hundred, so this is a genuine multi-day trip with more than four thousand seven hundred feet of gain before any climbing starts. Access depends entirely on the SR 20 winter closure, which shuts this stretch of highway from late November or early December until somewhere between mid April and early May, occasionally much later after a damaging winter.

sites.name: Mill Creek valley and the old Azurite Mine
sites.capacity: Unimproved. There is flat ground in the timber along the creek and open ground at the abandoned mine workings about five miles up from the trail junction, roughly eleven miles from the car. Room for a party or two in several places; nothing is built and nothing is maintained.
sites.water: Mill Creek runs alongside for most of the way and is the reliable supply on this side. Fill before leaving it for the climb toward the pass.
sites.permit: None. Dispersed camping on national forest land — no permit, no quota, no reservation. Fires are legal in the existing rings when no burn ban is in force, but forest-wide bans are routine from mid summer and the valley is dry, so plan on a stove. The mine workings are old industrial ground: leave the structures, timbers and hardware alone and do not go into any opening.
sites.notes: This is the honest middle of the western approach and the reason parties allow three days rather than two. The Mill Creek trail has had almost no use since the mine closed and it shows — long sections are faint, missing outright, or buried in slide alder, and the walking is slow, wet and scratchy in a way the mileage does not convey. The mine site itself is the natural first camp, open enough to dry gear and the last obvious flat ground before the climb. Beyond it the trail continues about three miles, and a party can either leave it near five thousand six hundred feet and climb the west slopes of Azurite directly, or carry on another mile and a half to Azurite Pass. Which of those you pick decides where the second night goes. Nobody should treat this valley as a trail walk; treat it as a bushwhack that occasionally has tread.

sites.name: Azurite Pass
sites.capacity: Open ground at and just below the pass, at around six thousand seven hundred feet — mapping and reports put it anywhere between about 6,680 and 6,750, so take the figure loosely. Room for a couple of small tents. Exposed, with no shelter and no windbreak worth the name.
sites.water: Seasonal snowmelt only, and not to be relied on late in the summer. The dependable sources are down in Mill Creek on the west side and in the Brush Creek drainage on the east. Fill low and carry it up; a party that arrives here dry in September has a problem.
sites.permit: None. National forest, dispersed camping, no permit and no quota. Camp on gravel or scree rather than the meadow. No fires — there is nothing to burn and a ban is likely in force anyway.
sites.notes: This is the hinge of the whole zone and the only camp that serves both summits well. Azurite Peak rises directly north of the pass and Mount Ballard stands about two miles further north again along the same ridge, so a party camped here can take Azurite by its south ridge and south-west gully and then continue to Ballard, or split the two across a pair of days. Both approaches converge on this spot, which is why it is worth carrying water and a tent this high rather than trying either peak from the valley. Reckon on the pass being under snow into July in a normal year and later after a heavy winter; the north-facing ground above it holds much longer. Weather comes across from the west with no warning here and there is no shelter for hours in any direction, so this is a camp to be conservative about.

sites.name: River Bend and Ballard campgrounds, Lost River Road
sites.capacity: Two small forested Forest Service campgrounds a short distance apart along the West Fork Methow, roughly eight to nine miles up the road from Mazama. Both are first come, first served only — there is no way to reserve and you must arrive in person to claim and pay for a site. Each is modest, so a summer weekend is a gamble.
sites.water: The river is right there. Treat these as basic sites and assume you will filter rather than find a working spigot.
sites.permit: No permit and no reservation, just a nightly fee paid on arrival. A Northwest Forest Pass is not needed to occupy a campsite, only to park at a trailhead. These are outside any wilderness, so none of the Pasayten self-issue paperwork applies.
sites.notes: These are the staging camps for the eastern approach and the comfortable answer to the night before. From Winthrop the drive runs west on SR 20 and then up the Lost River Road through Mazama to the end of the pavement, continuing a mile and a half or so on the gravel of the Harts Pass road. The West Fork Methow trailhead sits close by at around two thousand seven hundred feet, at a wooden fence just off a short spur. Being low and in timber, they are usable well before and after the high country is in condition, and they are far enough down the road that none of the Harts Pass driving difficulties apply. They also make a sensible base for a party that wants a look at the trail before committing to it, which on this side is worth doing — the West Fork Methow tread is badly overgrown and in poor repair, and the brush on the banks of the upper creeks is dense enough that the trail effectively disappears.

sites.name: Horse Heaven Camp, West Fork Methow
sites.capacity: An unimproved valley camp partway up the eastern approach, past the Trout Creek and Brush Creek junctions. Space for a party or two on flat ground in the timber. Nothing is maintained.
sites.water: Creek water close at hand, reliable through the season. This is the last comfortable water before the long climb to the pass, so fill completely here.
sites.permit: None. Dispersed national forest camping — no permit, no quota, no reservation. Northwest Forest Pass to park at the West Fork Methow trailhead. Fires only in an existing ring and only outside a burn ban, which by August usually means not at all.
sites.notes: This is the natural first night on the eastern approach to Azurite Pass and it breaks a walk that is otherwise too long to enjoy. From the trailhead near two thousand seven hundred feet the trail follows the West Fork Methow past Trout Creek and Brush Creek toward Jet Creek, and the camp sits partway along at about four thousand three hundred and fifty feet. Two warnings are worth taking seriously. The lower trail is overgrown and faint in places, though the tread improves as it climbs. And the brush on the banks of Jet Creek becomes extremely dense with no clear path through it at all, which is the section that costs parties hours and tempers. From here it is a sustained climb of well over two thousand feet to Azurite Pass and the peaks beyond, so leave early. Anyone weighing the two approaches should know they are about the same length and about equally neglected — pick by which side of the mountains you are driving from, not by hoping one has a better trail.
